text:
Ode imitated from Horace's O Navis, Referent.


What new hopes

carry you to the sea? Turn back,

turn back, audacious ship,

to your native shore.


You still see a thousand memories

of the past storm,

and already you fling yourself

a second time into fortune?


Your course is strewn with

stealthy shoals,

where too late the sounding line

will warn of dangers.


Ah! Turn back, there is still time,

while the sea caresses the shells

of the shore

with peaceful waves.


Soon, bristling into hills,

it will come battering the rocks,

and shipwrecked

relics make a carpet for Neptune.


The pretentious pomp

of silk streamers

does not fear the insults

of sonorous tempest.


What are bars and lions

against the Euro,

tyrant of the waves,

on your gilded stern?


What is your name, famous

in kingdoms of the dawn,

and where, for the sun,

its crystal chamber receives it?


Yesterday on these waters,

confident in itself,

another arrogant prow

challenged the wind;


and now, an ill-fated monument

that astonishes the sailor,

on a naked reef

it lies covered with algae.


What! Do you not hear me? Do you not alter

your course? Proudly choose

new sails,

and without fear put out to sea?


Do you not see, poor wretch,

that the sky is already clouding,

and the clouds, bellowing,

give birth to lightning?


Do you not see the hoary foam,

swollen into turmoil,

nor does the gale frighten you,

whistling in the rigging?


Turn back, beloved object

of my anxious concern;

turn back to the friendly shore,

before the sun goes down!

translation.title: To the Ship
translation.editorial_note: The translation preserves the Horatian ship ode, maritime warnings, and repeated appeals to turn back. This record is the valid ship-poem body; the neighboring “A Moisés” record is excluded for title mismatch.
